title: Almost (Acts 26)
hook: King Agrippa says almost thou persuadest me

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul arrested in the Temple, telling his story from the barracks steps. Your line was tell what happened.

Two years pass. Paul sits in custody in Caesarea, on the coast, while governors come and go. Then a new governor, Festus, gets a royal visit: King Agrippa and Bernice arrive with great pomp, the text says, with commanders and the city's leading men. Festus has a prisoner he doesn't know what to do with, and the king is curious. So Paul is brought in, in chains, to a hall full of power, and invited to speak.
screen: `TWO YEARS IN CAESAREA.` → `A KING ARRIVES WITH GREAT POMP.` → `A PRISONER IN A HALL OF POWER.`

segments.voice: Paul tells it again: the road, the light at midday brighter than the sun, the voice. This time he includes a line he hasn't mentioned before. The voice said, in the Douay-Rheims, "It is hard for thee to kick against the goad," like an ox kicking the stick that steers it. Paul had been fighting what was pulling him. He tells how he was sent to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light. Festus can't take it. He shouts: "Paul, thou art beside thyself: much learning doth make thee mad." Paul answers calmly, I am not mad, most noble Festus. Then he turns to the king. King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do. And Agrippa replies, in the Douay-Rheims: "In a little thou persuadest me to become a Christian." The King James turns that into almost, today's word. And there's Antioch's word, Christian, in a king's mouth. What did Agrippa mean? Honestly, nobody's sure. The Greek is two short words, en oligo, in a little. It could mean almost, or in such a short time, or with so little effort. He might be moved; he might be brushing Paul off with a smile. Paul's answer works either way: I would to God that, in a little and in much, not only you but all who hear me today might become such as I am, "except these bands." Picture him raising his chained hands. Then the king rises, and the hearing is over. This man could have gone free, Agrippa remarks, if he hadn't appealed to Caesar. So to Rome he goes.
screen: `HARD TO KICK AGAINST THE GOAD.` · `THOU ART BESIDE THYSELF.` · `IN A LITTLE THOU PERSUADEST ME.` · `EXCEPT THESE BANDS.` · then, large: `IN A LITTLE, AND IN MUCH.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've almost done for a long time: almost called, almost forgiven, almost started, almost gone to confession, or to Mass, or to the doctor. Name it quietly and notice what has kept it at almost, fear, pride, the schedule, a little embarrassment, then picture just the next small step that would move it from almost to altogether. If you pray, offer that one step.
Almost. King Agrippa's answer to Paul, maybe moved, maybe joking, and Paul's wish that all who heard him might become as he was. Today's word.
Your line: kick against the goad. Tomorrow, a storm at sea. Day five hundred fifty-six, done.

howItsDone: Catholics are encouraged to examine their consciences regularly, often at night, noticing what they have left undone as well as done, and many bring those things to the sacrament of reconciliation.

original.note: Greek: in a little. Agrippa's two words, which may mean almost, in so short a time, or with so little effort.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king nearly became a Christian.
what it means: Paul tells his story to a king, and the king's reply is so brief and slippery that nobody can say whether he was moved or mocking.
what a scholar hears: en oligō is ambiguous; the Douay keeps the Latin's in a little, while the King James reads almost. and Christian here is the name first heard in Antioch (Acts 11:26).

chat.says: When King Agrippa said Paul almost persuaded him, did he mean it?
options: Nobody's sure: the Greek, in a little, could mean almost, or he was brushing Paul off.
Yes, Agrippa was baptized by Paul in Caesarea later that very same week.
No, he was agreeing with Festus that all that learning had made Paul mad.
chat.meaning: Agrippa said, in a little thou persuadest me. The Greek could mean almost, or in so short a time; he may have been moved, or smiling.

goad.meaning: a pointed stick for steering an ox

notes: Confirm KJV wording of Acts 26:14, 26:24, 26:28 and 26:29.
Douay-Rheims 26:28 believed to read 'In a little thou persuadest me to become a Christian'; mentioned only as 'in a little', not quoted. Confirm.
'Two years in Caesarea' from Acts 24:27; confirm.
'Kick against the pricks' appears only in Acts 26:14 in critical texts (the KJV also has it at 9:5 from late manuscripts); the script says only that Paul hadn't mentioned it in his speech in Acts 22.
